items.stimulus: The 2019 survey of former warehouse employees reported three findings: median wages, which had risen by eleven percent; average weekly hours, which had barely changed; and the share of workers______ who said they would return to their old employer if offered the chance.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank is inside the third item, which begins after "; and." "Who said they would return..." tells you which workers are being counted, so it's essential to the meaning and takes no punctuation. Without it, "the share of workers" has no meaning. The first two items use ", which" because those clauses only add information, but this clause narrows down the group being counted.

B.why: This is a second-order trap. You copied the ", which" pattern from the earlier items. Here the clause defines the group being counted, and setting it off with a comma would make it sound as if all workers said they'd return.

C.why: You put a list semicolon at the blank, but the item boundary is the "; and" before "the share." A semicolon here would split one item into a phrase and a fragment.

D.why: A dash would set off the defining clause as an aside, cutting the counted group off from its description. Nothing closes the dash, either.

items.stimulus: Divers surveying the reef in 2024 counted four grazers that had returned after the marine heat wave: purple sea urchins; kelp crabs______ red abalone, which had been absent from the site for nine years; and a single school of opaleye, a fish rarely recorded north of the bay.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The text promises four grazers: urchins, kelp crabs, abalone, and opaleye. The separator after "urchins" is already a semicolon, and the abalone and opaleye items both contain internal commas, so every item must be separated by a semicolon. The blank falls between the second and third items.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. "Kelp crabs" and "red abalone" are both short, so a comma looked natural. The list already uses semicolons, and the later items have internal commas, so a comma here breaks the pattern.

B.why: A colon has already introduced the list. A second colon would make the abalone an explanation of the kelp crabs, not the next grazer.

D.why: "Kelp crabs and red abalone" turns two grazers into one item. With the final "; and," the list then has only three items, while the text says divers counted four.
